newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua's history scarred by war and dictators.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua's history scarred by war and dictators.

text.p: Nicaragua, which will be ruled from Friday by new President Arnoldo Aleman, has a turbulent history of civil war and dictatorships from which it has only recently begun to emerge.
The following is a brief chronology.
1838 -- Nicaragua gains independence from Spanish colonial rule. Country spends most of the 19th century in violent power struggles between Liberal and Conservative factions.
1909 -- U.S. government supports a coup by Nicaragua's conservative forces, beginning a long period of U.S. interventions and occupations in Nicaragua.
1927 -- Nicaragua's national hero, Cesar Augusto Sandino, begins a rebellion against the U.S. occupiers and their Nicaraguan allies.

1934 -- Sandino forces the U.S. marines to withdraw from Nicaragua. Sandino is assassinated even though he had laid down his arms. Anastasio Somoza Garcia, at the head of the National Guard, installs the Somoza family dynasty. Somoza and his sons Luis and Anastasio Jr. rule Nicaragua until 1979.
1972 -- Huge earthquake destroys most of central Managua.

1978 -- Somoza orders killing of Pedro Joaquin Chamorro, director of the newspaper La Prensa, unleashing a wave of public protests. Sandinista National Liberation Front assumes control of anti-Somoza fight and launches insurrection.

1979 -- Somoza flees the country, and a national reconstruction government is formed under Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega. Left-wing stance of Sandinista leaders results in formation of anti-Sandinista rebels, the Contras.

1984 -- Daniel Ortega is elected president in a vote boycotted by much of the opposition. The U.S. government led by President Ronald Reagan backs the Contras with arms and money, escalating the armed conflict.

Inflation reaches 33,000 percent in 1988 and GDP plunges 13.6 percent. Central American presidents step in and broker a peace settlement. The U.S. disarms the Contras in return for guarantees of a fair election.

1990 -- Violeta Barrios de Chamorro at the head of the 14-party anti-Sandinista National Opposition Union (UNO) coalition, defeats Daniel Ortega and is elected president. She installs a national reconciliation government, the war ends and the economy gradually starts to recover.

1996 -- Former right-wing Managua mayor Arnoldo Aleman, at the head of the four-party Liberal Alliance coalition, defeats Sandinista candidate Ortega in elections and takes power on Jan. 10, 1997. It is the second consecutive defeat at the ballot box for the Sandinistas, though they did manage to win almost 40 percent of the seats in the National Assembly and many city councils.
